scene: Fifth P erased in retrospect; Statius reveals his prodigality and secret faith; three poets reach the first tree of temperance
story: The angel of the fifth terrace has already brushed Dante's forehead and removed the fifth P when the canto opens. A shortened beatitude blesses those who thirst for justice, and the three poets climb more lightly. Only two P marks remain.

Virgil asks Statius why he was on the terrace of avarice. Statius corrects the assumption: his fault was prodigality, reckless expenditure, which is corrected on the same terrace as its opposite, hoarding.

Statius says Virgil's poetry had two formative effects: the Aeneid taught him the art of poetry, while the fourth Eclogue helped draw him toward Christian faith. He concealed his conversion out of fear and spent a long time on the terrace of sloth.
Virgil and Statius converse affectionately about Greek and Roman poets and figures dwelling in Limbo, while Dante listens with admiration.

At the sixth terrace, they find a strange tree shaped like an inverted fir, fragrant with fruit and watered by a clear stream falling from the cliff. A disembodied voice forbids eating and proclaims examples of temperance, including Mary at Cana, Daniel, and John the Baptist.
The poets continue beside the tree. The gluttony's discipline has begun, but no sixth P is removed in this canto.

semanticSomatic.semantic: An angelic cleansing already witnessed in narrative retrospect reduces marks to two, enabling lighter climbing
Opposite forms of imbalance can require correction on the same terrace; an inherited text can guide without controlling a reader
The poet receives evidence of the influence of his work while continuing as a companion and guide
The fruit's attraction and the spoken prohibition introduce temperance, not a meal

witnesses.action: RECALL the angel's recent touch and HEAR the beatitude while CLIMBING
witnesses.observable: Dante's fifth P is stated erased at the canto opening; count changes three to two

witnesses.action: HEAR Statius CLARIFY prodigality and RECOUNT Virgil's influence on poetry and belief
witnesses.observable: Statius's account is his testimony, not independent proof of another person's intention

witnesses.action: SEE the inverted tree and stream, HEAR the unseen voice, and REFRAIN from its fruit
witnesses.observable: the tree, water and injunction are encountered; gluttony remains to be cleansed

alchemicalReading: Possessiveness and wastefulness are opposite distortions of attachment. The fifth cleansing frees a measure of the burden while an inherited poem becomes a noncoercive source of guidance; the tree introduces disciplined desire.
invariant: The opening retrospectively establishes an angelic erasure from three to two P marks. Statius's correction concerns prodigality, not avarice; the tree does not remove another mark.
